title: Switching One Cell Type On or Off
endLine: Genetically switch one cell type on or off to test its role.

scenes.tts: How do you switch one cell type on or off in a living mouse? Many kinds of neurons sit tangled together in one tissue. Watching them fire shows when they act, not what they cause.
scenes.caption: How do you switch one cell type on or off in a living mouse? Many kinds of neurons sit tangled together in one tissue. Watching them fire shows when they act, not what they cause.
scenes.visual: Schematic neural circuit cutaway (labelled 'schematic', filling 65% of frame height): tangled grey neighbour neurons and blue target neurons connect a sensory input on the left to a behavioural readout panel on the right. Pulses ripple through all neurons together; before the narrator asks the question, the blue target neurons brighten with a bold question mark above them.
scenes.narration: How do you switch one cell type on or off in a living mouse? Many kinds of neurons sit tangled together in one tissue. Watching them fire shows when they act, not what they cause.

scenes.visual: The same schematic circuit pulses softly in place as the title 'Switching One Cell Type On or Off' appears in large high-contrast text, then fades smoothly back into the circuit.

scenes.tts: First, mouse genetics puts an actuator into one cell type. An actuator is an engineered protein that starts or stops cell activity. A stop flanked by lox P sites blocks the gene. Only cells making Cre recombinase delete that stop, switching it on permanently.
scenes.caption: First, mouse genetics puts an actuator into one cell type. An actuator is an engineered protein that starts or stops cell activity. A stop flanked by loxP sites blocks the gene. Only cells making Cre recombinase delete that stop, switching it on permanently.
scenes.visual: Same schematic circuit (labelled 'schematic'): a DNA strip unfolds directly from the circuit showing a red STOP block between two loxP triangles ahead of an actuator gene. In grey neighbour cells, the STOP stays shut and the gene stays dark. In blue target cells, Cre recombinase arrives first, snips out the STOP block, and the actuator gene glows blue as switches appear on the blue cells.
scenes.narration: First, mouse genetics puts an actuator into one cell type. An actuator is an engineered protein that starts or stops cell activity. A stop flanked by loxP sites blocks the gene. Only cells making Cre recombinase delete that stop, switching it on permanently.

scenes.tts: In chemogenetics, targeted cells build a dread: a designer receptor activated only by a synthetic ligand. That ligand drifts through tissue but ignores every other cell. Driving the targeted cells tests whether they are sufficient for a response. Quieting them tests whether they are necessary.
scenes.caption: In chemogenetics, targeted cells build a DREADD: a designer receptor activated only by a synthetic ligand. That ligand drifts through tissue but ignores every other cell. Driving the targeted cells tests whether they are sufficient for a response. Quieting them tests whether they are necessary.
scenes.visual: Same schematic circuit (labelled 'schematic', no molecular structures): stylized cup-shaped designer receptors appear only on the blue target cells. Synthetic ligand dots drift across the whole tissue, bouncing off grey neighbours and docking only into the blue receptors. First, the blue cells brighten and drive the right-hand readout ('Sufficient?'). Next, an inhibitory state dims the blue cells during incoming input ('Necessary?').
scenes.narration: In chemogenetics, targeted cells build a DREADD: a designer receptor activated only by a synthetic ligand. That ligand drifts through tissue but ignores every other cell. Driving the targeted cells tests whether they are sufficient for a response. Quieting them tests whether they are necessary.

scenes.tts: Genetic silencing can also quiet cells without a designer receptor. You can silence transmitter release, or permanently remove cells, called ablation, with diphtheria toxin. Reversible inhibition tests whether cells are needed right now. A genetic switch turns one cell type on or off to test its role.
scenes.caption: Genetic silencing can also quiet cells without a designer receptor. You can silence transmitter release, or permanently remove cells, called ablation, with diphtheria toxin. Reversible inhibition tests whether cells are needed right now. A genetic switch turns one cell type on or off to test its role.
scenes.visual: Same schematic circuit (labelled 'schematic'): first, transmitter dots freeze at the blue terminals; next, a 'Diphtheria toxin' drop makes the blue cells vanish permanently ('Ablation'). Then the blue cells return and dim temporarily under the synthetic ligand ('Reversible'). A clean label below reads 'Switch on or off: test the role'.
scenes.narration: Genetic silencing can also quiet cells without a designer receptor. You can silence transmitter release, or permanently remove cells, called ablation, with diphtheria toxin. Reversible inhibition tests whether cells are needed right now. A genetic switch turns one cell type on or off to test its role.

scenes.tts: Pause and predict. Suppose excitatory spinal neurons help drive defensive responses to mechanical touch. You put an inhibitory designer receptor in those neurons and give the ligand. Should the force needed to make the mouse pull away rise or fall?
scenes.caption: Pause and predict. Suppose excitatory spinal neurons help drive defensive responses to mechanical touch. You put an inhibitory designer receptor in those neurons and give the ligand. Should the force needed to make the mouse pull away rise or fall?
scenes.visual: Same schematic circuit (labelled 'schematic'), now tagged 'Spinal cord': blue excitatory neurons display inhibitory designer receptors as synthetic ligand dots dock onto them. On the left, a schematic mechanical touch probe approaches; on the right, a schematic 'Force to pull away' gauge shows a bold question mark between up and down arrows.
scenes.narration: Pause and predict. Suppose excitatory spinal neurons help drive defensive responses to mechanical touch. You put an inhibitory designer receptor in those neurons and give the ligand. Should the force needed to make the mouse pull away rise or fall?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause (4.5 seconds): the schematic spinal circuit holds with gentle ambient drift on the docked ligand dots while the question 'Force to pull away: rise or fall?' stays bright on screen and the gauge arrows pulse slowly.

scenes.tts: It rises. Quieting those excitatory neurons makes the mouse less sensitive to mechanical touch. Its mechanical withdrawal threshold rises, meaning it takes stronger force before the mouse pulls away.
scenes.caption: It rises. Quieting those excitatory neurons makes the mouse less sensitive to mechanical touch. Its mechanical withdrawal threshold rises, meaning it takes stronger force before the mouse pulls away.
scenes.visual: Same schematic spinal circuit (labelled 'schematic'): the ligand-bound blue neurons dim, the outgoing signal arrow narrows, and the schematic 'Withdrawal threshold' gauge rises smoothly to a higher level labelled 'Takes stronger force'.
scenes.narration: It rises. Quieting those excitatory neurons makes the mouse less sensitive to mechanical touch. Its mechanical withdrawal threshold rises, meaning it takes stronger force before the mouse pulls away.

scenes.tts: Genetic tools can mislead. Cre marking is permanent, capturing any cell that ever expressed the driver. Drivers can be leaky in wrong cells, or mosaic, missing target cells. Reporter light misses leftover target protein, so measure driver range and target loss directly in tissue.
scenes.caption: Genetic tools can mislead. Cre marking is permanent, capturing any cell that ever expressed the driver. Drivers can be leaky in wrong cells, or mosaic, missing target cells. Reporter light misses leftover target protein, so measure driver range and target loss directly in tissue.
scenes.visual: Same schematic circuit (labelled 'schematic'): error states animate in place on the cell cluster. First, a past-expressing neighbour stays permanently tinted ('Past expression'). Next, a stray grey neuron lights up ('Leaky') while two blue target neurons stay dark ('Mosaic'). Finally, a bright reporter halo fades to show direct tissue verification of driver range and target loss.
scenes.narration: Genetic tools can mislead. Cre marking is permanent, capturing any cell that ever expressed the driver. Drivers can be leaky in wrong cells, or mosaic, missing target cells. Reporter light misses leftover target protein, so measure driver range and target loss directly in tissue.

scenes.tts: With those checks, these tools unlocked key findings. In 2013, Vrontou and colleagues put a dread in M R G P R B four neurons. Activating those hairy-skin sensory neurons gave male mice conditioned place preference. They spent more time in the chamber paired with activation.
scenes.caption: With those checks, these tools unlocked key findings. In 2013, Vrontou and colleagues put a DREADD in MrgprB4 neurons. Activating those hairy-skin sensory neurons gave male mice conditioned place preference. They spent more time in the chamber paired with activation.
scenes.visual: Same schematic circuit (labelled 'schematic') shifts to hairy skin on the left: ligand dots activate designer receptors on blue MrgprB4 sensory neurons. On the right, a schematic two-chamber box shows a mouse spending more time in the lit chamber paired with activation ('Conditioned place preference', Vrontou et al., 2013).
scenes.narration: With those checks, these tools unlocked key findings. In 2013, Vrontou and colleagues put a DREADD in MrgprB4 neurons. Activating those hairy-skin sensory neurons gave male mice conditioned place preference. They spent more time in the chamber paired with activation.

scenes.tts: In 2014, Duan and colleagues ablated spinal somatostatin-lineage neurons with diphtheria toxin. Four weeks later, tissue counts confirmed depletion. Controls averaged one hundred five plus or minus four neurons per lumbar hemisection. Ablated mice fell to seventeen plus or minus two. Those are averages across three mice per group, plus their uncertainty. Ablation impaired acute and injury-associated mechanical defensive behaviour.
scenes.caption: In 2014, Duan and colleagues ablated spinal somatostatin-lineage neurons with diphtheria toxin. Four weeks later, tissue counts confirmed depletion. Controls averaged 105 ± 4 neurons per lumbar hemisection. Ablated mice fell to 17 ± 2. Those are averages across three mice per group, plus their uncertainty. Ablation impaired acute and injury-associated mechanical defensive behaviour.
scenes.visual: Same schematic spinal circuit (labelled 'schematic') compresses slightly to make room for a computed bar chart from Duan et al. (2014) (4 weeks after diphtheria toxin, 15 to 17 lumbar hemisections, 3 mice per group): 'Control' at 105 ± 4 labelled somatostatin-lineage neurons per hemisection drops to 'Ablated' at 17 ± 2 (mean ± SEM). Beside it, the schematic mechanical defensive response gauge drops.
scenes.narration: In 2014, Duan and colleagues ablated spinal somatostatin-lineage neurons with diphtheria toxin. Four weeks later, tissue counts confirmed depletion. Controls averaged 105 ± 4 neurons per lumbar hemisection. Ablated mice fell to 17 ± 2. Those are averages across three mice per group, plus their uncertainty. Ablation impaired acute and injury-associated mechanical defensive behaviour.

scenes.tts: Reversible tools strengthen a different inference. In 2016, Christensen and colleagues used chemogenetic inhibition on spinal somatostatin neurons in naive mice. Mechanical withdrawal thresholds rose, and thermal withdrawal latency lengthened, so mice took longer to pull away. Switching one genetic cell type on or off tests what it actually does.

scenes.visual: Same schematic spinal circuit (labelled 'schematic'): the somatostatin neurons remain intact and dim reversibly under synthetic ligand (Christensen et al., 2016). On the right, two schematic gauges rise smoothly in sync: 'Mechanical threshold' and 'Thermal latency'.

scenes.visual: The schematic circuit fades to a clean end card showing only the take-home sentence verbatim in large high-contrast text: 'Genetically switch one cell type on or off to test its role.'
